name: Colorado Midland Railway
basis: East of Divide the line is one continuous route of 26.82 miles to Colorado Springs, from a tracing supplied by the atlas's owner and tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 83 per cent of it lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_cm_east.py). The Midland Terminal's timetables give 26.9 miles for the same run. Through the tunnel district above Manitou, 17 to 20 miles from Divide, the test reads poorly because of the tunnels themselves; seven tunnel points marked on a supplied map all lie within about 120 ft of the route there. West of Divide the line is one continuous route of 13.47 miles through Florissant to the edge of the region, from the line 'Divide to Leadville' in a Google Earth file supplied by the owner, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 92 per cent on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent (see atlas/tools/once_route_cm_west.py). About a mile and a half near its west end has no lidar held and is untested.
notes: From Poor's manuals: chartered 23 November 1883; construction begun April 1886 and 100 miles completed by 1 July 1887, which covers the line up Ute Pass; road opened throughout 15 October 1888; receivers appointed 1 February 1894; sold under foreclosure 8 September 1897 and succeeded by the Colorado Midland Railway, chartered 11 October 1897. The end is still from secondary sources, which disagree: operations stopped in August 1918, the line was abandoned in 1921 and the company dissolved in 1922. East of Divide the track passed to the Midland Terminal: its timetable of 7 September 1920 already runs from Colorado Springs. Those segments are dated to 1949.

name: Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District Railway (the Short Line)
basis: From the edge of Colorado Springs to Cameron the line is one continuous route of 36.97 miles, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 90 per cent of what could be tested lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_shortline.py). It is the OpenStreetMap pieces put in order, with two gaps (1.1 and 6.2 miles) followed along Gold Camp Road, which runs on the grade. Against the timetable of 26 September 1909, Duffields, Rosemont and Cameron Junction each fall 2.9 to 3.0 miles later on the route than their printed miles from Colorado Springs Yard, so the route's length agrees with the timetable to a tenth of a mile over 21 miles, and it begins about 3 miles out from the yard: that first stretch through Colorado Springs is not traced. Part of the route has no 1 m lidar and is untested. West of Cameron the pieces are as OpenStreetMap has them. West of Cameron the main line into Cripple Creek (by Hoosier Pass, Fairview and Poverty Gulch) is a trace of 4.12 miles from the USGS district map surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), which letters it with the railway's name. It is inferred and good to about 200 ft at best: 8 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, because east of Poverty Gulch all of it is now inside the open-pit mine. Its length has no clean check: Poor's 1902 gives 45.82 miles from Colorado Springs to Cripple Creek and the 1909 timetable puts Cameron Junction 39.5 miles from the yard, which would make this run about 6.3 miles against roughly 4.6 traced; the two figures are counted from different points and the difference is not explained (see atlas/tools/once_route_district.py). The branch from Cameron to Victor and the electric lines are not traced. Other pieces west of Cameron are as OpenStreetMap has them. Through Goldfield a surviving bench of 1.67 miles is entered as part of the branch from Cameron to Victor: 96 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, so the bench is measured. That it was this railway's is inferred from the Sanborn sheet of December 1908, which letters a track 'C. S. & C. C. D. R.R. Short Line' where the bench crosses the town, and from the USGS map surveyed in 1894, which has the Midland Terminal west of Goldfield and no railway here (see atlas/tools/once_route_goldfield.py). Its top is where it meets the Midland Terminal's line below Independence; this railway's own track from Cameron down to that point, and the last 0.6 mile into Victor, are not traced.
notes: From Poor's 1902: chartered 13 April 1897 as the Cripple Creek District Railway, present name adopted 17 November 1897; the electric line from Cripple Creek to Victor opened 1 January 1898, the line via Anaconda 9 September 1900, 'the other lines in 1901'; main line Colorado Springs to Cripple Creek 45.82 miles; standard gauge. From Moody's 1917: leased to the Florence and Cripple Creek from the Colorado and Southern on 1 November 1911. Still from secondary sources: the opening day of 8 April 1901, and the end, about 1920, with the rails lifted by 1922 and the grade sold for a toll road, later Gold Camp Road.

name: Midland Terminal Railway
basis: From Divide to the end of the surviving trace near Independence the line is one continuous route of 21.76 miles, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 94 per cent of it lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_mt.py). It is the OpenStreetMap pieces put in order, with two gaps between Divide and Midland crossed by a line found from the lidar. The timetables put Gillett 14.4 and Cameron 19.7 miles from Divide; the route puts them at 14.6 and 19.8. Beyond Independence the line to Victor and Cripple Creek is not traced. A separate OpenStreetMap piece running south-west from Gillett is kept as it was; what it is has not been established. Between Cripple Creek and Victor (by Anaconda, Beacon Hill, Elkton and Eclipse) the line is a trace of 5.58 miles from the USGS district map surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), inferred and good to about 200 ft at best: only 1 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, because most of that ground is now the open-pit mine. The timetable of 1920 gives 5.3 miles for the same run. Where the map draws several railways side by side the trace is not told apart from the Florence and Cripple Creek's (see atlas/tools/once_route_district.py). Into Victor the upper of the map's two lines is taken as this railway's: the key maps of the Sanborn sheets of August 1900 and December 1908 letter the upper line Midland Terminal, with a switchback, and the lower Florence and Cripple Creek. The 1903 map draws no railway along the separate OpenStreetMap piece running south-west from Gillett, which follows the present highway; it is kept only until that is settled. Below Independence the line is carried 1.87 miles toward Victor (26 per cent of it on a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, all of that in the first half mile). The first half mile, a horseshoe, is a surviving bench that the Divide route meets within 2 m, and the USGS map surveyed in 1894 letters the Midland Terminal on a line of that shape: bench measured, attribution inferred. Beyond it, along the east foot of Battle Mountain and west past the Portland mine, only the corridor is drawn, good to about 300 ft: the 1903 map has three to five unnamed tracks side by side there and the ground is reworked. The descent into Victor by the switchback is not traced (see atlas/tools/once_route_mt_victor_side.py).
notes: Incorporated 9 August 1892 under Colorado laws; 29.4 miles from Divide to Cripple Creek with a branch to Victor; controlled by the Cripple Creek Central from 1904 (Moody's 1917). The timetable of 14 July 1895 runs Divide, Gillett, Grassy, Independence, Victor, with a stage from Grassy to Cripple Creek; by the table of 26 September 1909 Cripple Creek is a station at 30 miles. From 1920 the tables run from Colorado Springs; from January 1945 they are marked freight service only; the last read is March 1948. Still from secondary sources: rails to Midland in December 1893 and Gillett on 4 July 1894, into Cripple Creek in December 1895, last run February 1949. The drawn line is dated from 1894.

From the horseshoe along the east foot of Battle Mountain and west past the Portland mine, 1.38 miles: the corridor only. Traced from the USGS map of 1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), which draws three to five tracks side by side here and names none; the map surveyed in 1894 draws one, lettered Midland Terminal, on the same hillside. The trace follows one drawn track and is moved 76 m to start on the bench. On the 1 m lidar 0% of it reads as a smooth grade; the ground is reworked by mine roads. It stops above Victor: the descent to the depot, by a switchback, is not traced.

name: Florence and Cripple Creek Railroad
basis: Between Cripple Creek and Victor the line is a trace of 6.11 miles from the USGS district map surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), inferred: 13 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar. For about a mile south of Cripple Creek it is laid on the bench the tourist railway now uses, which the map's line follows at a typical 45 m; the rest is good to about 200 ft at best and lies mostly in ground now mined. The timetable of 2 June 1895 gives 5.7 miles from Cripple Creek to Victor. Where the map draws several railways side by side the trace is not told apart from the Midland Terminal's (see atlas/tools/once_route_district.py). South of Victor the line to Florence is not traced; two tunnels in Phantom Canyon are from OpenStreetMap.
notes: Narrow gauge (3 ft). Poor's 1895 gives incorporation on 11 May 1893; Poor's 1899 says chartered 10 May 1893 and road opened 1 September 1894; Florence to Cripple Creek 40.3 miles. Moody's 1917: dissolved 1 May 1915, its assets conveyed to the Golden Circle Railroad, renamed the Cripple Creek and Colorado Springs. Secondary sources give other days (first train into Cripple Creek 1 July 1894; dissolved 27 April 1915) and the flood of 21 July 1912 that wrecked the canyon line; the drawn tunnels are dated to 1912 on that account.
